paragraphs.heading: Carbon in a crystal
paragraphs.text: Diamond is a mineral form of the element carbon. Its atoms are arranged in a crystal structure called diamond cubic. It is a strong but brittle solid with no taste or smell. It conducts electricity poorly, does not dissolve in water, and has no color in its pure form.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is so hard
paragraphs.text: Solid carbon comes in different forms, called allotropes, depending on the type of chemical bond. Diamond and graphite are the two most common allotropes of pure carbon. In diamond each atom is bound to four nearest neighbors, and the atoms form tetrahedra. Tetrahedra are rigid, the bonds are strong, and diamond has more atoms per unit volume than any other known substance. That is why diamond is the hardest and also the least compressible.

paragraphs.heading: The same element, much softer
paragraphs.text: In graphite the atoms form planes, and each atom is bound to three nearest neighbors. The bonds between those neighbors are even stronger than in diamond. The bonds between one plane and the next are weak, though, so the planes easily slip past each other. As a result graphite is much softer than diamond.

paragraphs.heading: Made deep in the Earth
paragraphs.text: Most natural diamonds are between 1 billion and 3.5 billion years old. Most formed in the Earth's mantle at depths of 150 to 250 kilometres, though a few came from as deep as 800 kilometres. Under high pressure and temperature, fluids containing carbon dissolved various minerals and replaced them with diamonds. Much more recently, hundreds to tens of millions of years ago, volcanic eruptions carried them to the surface and left them in igneous rocks known as kimberlites and lamproites.

paragraphs.heading: Why diamond does not turn to graphite
paragraphs.text: At room temperature and pressure, graphite is the chemically stable form of carbon. Diamond is metastable, with a significant energy barrier that its atoms must get over to reach the lower energy state. Its conversion to graphite goes at a negligible rate, on a timescale of millions to billions of years. Above about 4500 K, however, diamond turns into graphite rapidly.

paragraphs.heading: Where the colors come from
paragraphs.text: The arrangement of atoms in diamond is extremely rigid, so few types of impurity can get into it; boron and nitrogen are two exceptions. A small number of impurities or defects, about one per million lattice atoms, can color a diamond. Boron gives blue, nitrogen gives yellow, defects give brown, and exposure to radiation gives green.

paragraphs.heading: Proving it is carbon
paragraphs.text: In 1772 Antoine Lavoisier, a French scientist, took a lens and focused the sun's rays on a diamond in an atmosphere of oxygen. The only product of the burning was carbon dioxide, which proved that diamond is made of carbon. In 1797 the English chemist Smithson Tennant repeated the experiment and expanded it. He showed that burning diamond and burning graphite give off the same amount of gas, which established that the two substances are chemically equivalent.

paragraphs.heading: Tools and synthetic diamonds
paragraphs.text: No natural material is harder than diamond or has a higher thermal conductivity, and industry puts these properties to major use in tools for cutting and polishing. Diamonds can also be grown. Synthetic ones start from carbon of high purity held at high pressures and temperatures, or from hydrocarbon gases in a process called chemical vapor deposition (CVD). Natural and synthetic diamonds are most often told apart with optical techniques or by measuring thermal conductivity.
